## Today

Theory is the part of this course that sounds least useful and turns out to decide the
most. It is what tells you which of the thousands of chat messages in front of you are
worth counting.

You leave today with a lens picked for your own project, and a reason for picking it that
you could say out loud to somebody who disagreed.

## One finding, three explanations

Livestream viewing looks more socially motivated than content motivated. Why?

- **Uses and gratifications** (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973): viewers are active agents
  meeting a social need a finished video cannot
- **Parasocial interaction** (Horton & Wohl, 1956): viewers form one-sided bonds with the
  streamer, and connection is how that bond feels
- **Social identity** (Tajfel & Turner, 1979): the community is a group, and chat is a
  space of belonging

Same pattern, three research programs, three different studies.

## Theory is not speculation

- In casual use "theory" means guess. In research it means the opposite of a guess.
- A **theory** is a formal, systematic explanation of relationships between concepts
- **Logically coherent:** the parts fit together without contradiction
- **Generalizable:** it applies across contexts rather than to one case
- **Falsifiable:** it makes predictions that could turn out wrong
- **Generative:** it produces new hypotheses rather than closing the question

## Social identity, worked

Tajfel and Turner (1979) held that people take part of their self-concept from the groups
they belong to. Watch what that produces:

- Viewers rate their preferred community above rivals, especially on subjective dimensions
  like authenticity
- Criticize a streamer and the regulars respond defensively
- In a different domain entirely: partisans rate aligned news outlets as more credible even
  when the factual content is identical

One idea, three predictions, all of them checkable.

## The lens metaphor

- Theory works like a camera lens. Some things come sharp, some fall outside the frame.
- **Appraisal theory** focuses you on individual evaluation, so you build surveys and
  experiments measuring personal reactions
- **Social identity** focuses you on group meaning, so you analyze how members talk about
  the stream as a marker of who they are
- Same phenomenon, different designs, and **neither one is wrong**
- You cannot use every lens at once. Trying produces blur, not depth.

- Which of the three lenses would you use, and what would it make you look at?
- What would that lens push out of the frame, and does losing it matter?

*Two minutes with a neighbor, then we compare.*

## Three paradigms

- **Social scientific:** an objective reality that can be observed and measured. Deductive,
  so you start from theory and test. Asks *does X cause Y?*
- **Interpretive:** reality is built through interaction. Inductive, so you observe and
  build theory from what you find. Asks *what does X mean to the people who live it?*
  Methods include grounded theory and thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006).
- **Critical and cultural:** power shapes what counts as knowledge. Asks *whose interests
  does X serve, and whose voices go unheard?*

## Grand and middle-range

- **Grand theories** explain human behaviour across every context: Marxism, psychoanalysis,
  structuralism
- Intellectually powerful, and close to untestable. The scope is too wide and the
  predictions too general to be proven wrong.
- **Middle-range theories** are specific enough to generate testable hypotheses and broad
  enough to travel past one case
- Robert Merton named the zone. Every theory in the catalogue ahead sits in it.

## Catalogue: relationship and group

- **Parasocial interaction** (Horton & Wohl, 1956): one-sided bonds with media figures that
  feel intimate but are not reciprocated. Predicts stronger connection with more
  consumption, and a sense of betrayal when a scandal breaks. The lens for donations to
  strangers, and for influencer marketing.
- **Social identity** (Tajfel & Turner, 1979): group membership shapes self-concept.
  Predicts in-group favouritism and symbolic boundary keeping. Foundational in political
  communication and sports fandom.

## Catalogue: media and message

- **Agenda setting** (McCombs & Shaw, 1972): media do not tell people what to think, they
  tell people what to think about. On Twitch the front page, the recommendations, and the
  category rankings are all setting an agenda.
- **Framing** (Goffman, 1974; Entman, 1993): how information is presented shapes how it is
  read. Episodic framing pushes blame toward individuals, thematic framing toward
  structures. You can see it in how streamers title their own broadcasts.

## Catalogue: audience and exposure

- **Uses and gratifications** (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973): audiences are active and
  pick media to meet needs. Sjöblom and Hamari (2017) used it directly to study why people
  watch other people play video games.
- **Cultivation** (Gerbner & Gross, 1976): long-term cumulative exposure shapes how people
  perceive social reality. Heavy consumers overestimate what they keep seeing, most
  strongly where they have no direct experience to check it against.

## Two lenses on the same chat

Four messages from one Twitch broadcast:

> **DragoBoi89:** xQc actually playing well today wtf
>
> **emotelord:** PogU PogU
>
> **realnamedfan:** @xqcow do u remember when u said hi to me last week
>
> **streamfan22:** chat is this real

Read them once before we put a lens on them.

## Two readings

- **Uses and gratifications:** four needs, four viewers. Evaluative commentary, collective
  emotional expression, direct acknowledgement, collective sense-making. All four are
  equally interesting to this lens.
- **Parasocial interaction:** realnamedfan is the case. An @-address plus a memory claim
  about a previous acknowledgement treats a one-sided interaction as a continuing
  relationship.
- emotelord and streamfan22 never address the streamer, so this lens pushes them to the
  edges. Same four messages. Two different studies.

## Four methods, four questions

- **Surveys** measure what people report. Natural for uses and gratifications, and limited
  by the gap between what people say and what they do.
- **Experiments** isolate cause by manipulating something. Natural for "does X cause Y?",
  and limited by artificiality.
- **Qualitative methods** capture meaning and lived experience. Natural for the interpretive
  question, and they trade breadth for depth.
- **Content analysis** quantifies features of the content itself, at a scale nobody could
  eyeball.

## Why content analysis here

Three reasons, and none of them is that it is the best method:

- **Fit:** the Twitch data *is* content, millions of messages and stream records
- **Pedagogical completeness:** you practise operationalization, sampling, reliability, and
  analysis on one dataset, without having to recruit a single human subject
- **Transfer:** a precise codebook, tested reliability, and systematic sampling are what
  make every other method work too

Choosing with the alternatives in view beats choosing by default.
